case_study_insert.main_stem: Meridian Health Partners (MHP) is a private limited company in the private healthcare sector, based in the Dublin region and running day-case surgery clinics, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2012 by Dr Aisha Rahman, it receives referrals from local GP practices and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MHP plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new endoscopic day-surgery suite with sterile single-use procedure packs, financed by a $750,000 ten-year bank loan and $450,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $42, and produces 60,000 units a year. MHP faces a rising instrument reprocessing defect rate of 3.4% and nurse absenteeism of 11%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Log — Q4 2025: The day-surgery suite completed 14,500 procedure packs last quarter at a reprocessing defect rate of 3.4%, up from 1.9% a year earlier. Patient complaint letters rose from 18 to 31 a month. Average pre-op waiting time is 6.4 days. A survey of 500 patients found 68% would pay $15 more for a private same-day slot, and 57% choose clinics with published infection-control rates. A skills audit shows 24 of 80 clinical staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new endoscope reprocessors; off-the-job training courses in infection control at the regional college cost $620 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Meridian Health Partners for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Healthcare Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.80 to $14.60 per hour from April 2026, lifting payroll costs for clinical support staff. (3) Sterile-pack and disposable-kit input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while patient demand for same-day surgery slots grew 3.2%.

questions.question_text: MHP is funding part of its $1,200,000 day-surgery suite with a $750,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MHP of using the $450,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit has no interest charge or compulsory repayment, so MHP keeps the cash flow needed to meet fixed costs of $480,000 a year while it services the $750,000 loan. Every dollar not handed to the bank can absorb the 9.6% rise in sterile-pack costs, helping MHP hold its $42 selling price and keep the day-surgery suite competitive for the local GP practices that refer patients.

Point 2: Using $450,000 retained profit avoids further collateral and protects Dr Aisha Rahman's ownership. The $1,200,000 suite cannot be repossessed if demand for the 60,000 units falls short, and the survey finding that 68% of 500 patients would pay $15 more for a same-day slot gives MHP confidence to fund the launch from internal resources rather than increase debt. With nurse absenteeism at 11% and a 3.4% reprocessing defect rate already raising costs, that flexibility matters because loan interest must be paid however many procedure packs are actually delivered. Internal funds also avoid lender conditions on how the suite is run.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to MHP's financing decision and its day-surgery operations.

questions.question_text: MHP is promoting its new endoscopic day-surgery suite. Consider national television advertising, partnerships with local GP practices, or social media campaigns. Which should MHP choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: TV would build rapid, mass awareness of the new $1,200,000 suite across the Dublin region and make the same-day slot offer familiar to thousands of viewers. The drawback is cost and waste: airtime and production are expensive for a business with fixed costs of $480,000 and a $750,000 loan, and most viewers are outside MHP's referral network of local GP practices, so the spend would not convert into the 14,500 procedure packs delivered last quarter.

Partnerships with local GP practices: GPs already refer patients to MHP, so formal links, shared leaflets and short practice presentations would reach precisely the people who need day-case surgery. This route is cheap, uses the 68% of 500 surveyed patients who would pay $15 more for a same-day slot, and can highlight the published infection-control rates that 57% of respondents check. It is slower to build than a TV campaign and depends on GPs' willingness to promote one provider, but it fits MHP's hierarchical referral relationships.

Social media campaigns: Targeted adverts can show the new suite, display infection-control data and drive direct bookings, with measurable clicks against the 6.4-day pre-op waiting time. They are cheaper than television and reach younger patients, but clinical choices are trust-heavy and online leads are less credible than a GP recommendation, so conversion may be low and the message competes with many other providers.

Recommendation: MHP should choose partnerships with local GP practices, supported by a small social media campaign for appointment reminders. This is the cheapest option, builds on existing referrals and matches the 57% who check infection-control rates. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for an 80-staff clinic servicing a $750,000 loan; social media alone is rejected because it lacks the clinical trust that a GP endorsement supplies.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to MHP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MHP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MHP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and social media are rejected.

questions.question_text: MHP's instrument reprocessing defect rate has risen to 3.4% and nurse absenteeism to 11%. Explain two benefits for MHP of using democratic leadership with its workforce of 80.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 80 staff to suggest how the new endoscope reprocessors should be run, raising ownership of infection-control routines. Operators who help set reprocessing checks are more likely to follow them consistently, directly attacking the 3.4% defect rate that has risen from 1.9% and protecting the 14,500 procedure packs completed last quarter; this matters inside MHP's hierarchical structure, where front-line views can otherwise be lost.

Point 2: Involvement raises job satisfaction and reduces the 11% nurse absenteeism, because staff who are consulted are more committed to their shifts. Better attendance keeps pre-op waiting time near 6.4 days and cuts the need to retrain the 24 of 80 clinical staff missing on-the-job training at $620 each, protecting the $42 selling price and the return on the $1,200,000 suite. Inside a hierarchical structure this upward flow of ideas is especially useful because it brings front-line detail to managers who may not see every reprocessing cycle, so the $620 college course becomes a backup rather than an immediate cost.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MHP's defect rate, absenteeism, training and expansion.

questions.question_text: MHP must train 24 of 80 clinical staff who have not completed on-the-job training on the new endoscope reprocessors. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should MHP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching beside the new endoscope reprocessors is specific to MHP's own infection-control routines and costs no course fees, while the 24 trainees continue to support the 14,500 procedure packs delivered last quarter. Supervisors can correct technique immediately, which is the fastest way to push the 3.4% reprocessing defect rate back toward 1.9%. The drawbacks are that experienced staff lose time from their own duties, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no external certificate when inspectors ask for published infection-control evidence.

Off-the-job training: The regional college course at $620 per employee costs 24 × $620 = $14,880 in total, small beside the $1,200,000 suite. It gives structured, up-to-date infection-control knowledge and a recognised certificate that supports the 57% of patients who check published rates. However, it removes 24 of 80 clinical staff from the clinic, which could lengthen the 6.4-day pre-op wait and worsen 11% absenteeism elsewhere, and generic teaching still needs adaptation to MHP's actual machines.

Decision: MHP should choose on-the-job training first, with a short certified college module later for senior operators. On-the-job coaching is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids worsening output while absenteeism is already 11%. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because losing 24 staff from an 80-strong workforce would delay the 14,500-pack schedule and the $14,880 fee is harder to justify before the 3.4% defect rate is brought under control. With reprocessing defects already at 3.4%, immediate correction on the actual machines is worth more than classroom theory. MHP should compare that rate before and after a pilot shift and spend the $14,880 only if on-the-job coaching leaves a gap.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MHP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of MHP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and infection-control relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MHP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $480,000 ÷ ($42 − $18) = $480,000 ÷ $24 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $42 − $18 = $24. Answer: contribution per unit is $24.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MHP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 20,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 60,000 units gives a margin of safety of 40,000 units, showing how far same-day demand could fall before the suite loses money.
2. Contribution per unit of $24 lets managers test pricing: a $2 discount from $42 to $40 leaves $22 contribution, so they can judge whether extra same-day volume still covers the $480,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs and contribution helps set the volume needed to service the $750,000 bank loan, checking the $1,200,000 suite can meet repayments before MHP commits more capital.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost, $480,000 ÷ 60,000 units = $8 plus $18 = $26 a pack, across quarters to spot the 3.4% reprocessing defect rate and the 11% nurse absenteeism driving extra costs.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $24 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 40,000-unit safety margin against 60,000-unit output; discount pricing from $42 against $24 contribution; loan-service volume for the $750,000 borrowing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $26 to tackle reprocessing defects and absenteeism.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MHP's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has MHP's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 14.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 16.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $1,200,000 came from $3,000,000 revenue less $1,800,000 cost of sales, so $1,200,000 ÷ $3,000,000 × 100 = 40.0. In 2025, $3,600,000 revenue less $2,016,000 cost of sales gives $1,584,000, so $1,584,000 ÷ $3,600,000 × 100 = 44.0. Operating profit of $420,000 in 2024 and $576,000 in 2025 divided by revenue gives $420,000 ÷ $3,000,000 × 100 = 14.0 and $576,000 ÷ $3,600,000 × 100 = 16.0. Returns on capital were $420,000 ÷ $2,800,000 × 100 = 15.0 in 2024 and $576,000 ÷ $3,200,000 × 100 = 18.0 in 2025. Interest payable rose from $60,000 to $75,000, so the gain was not caused by cheaper borrowing.

Evaluation: Every indicator moved favourably. The gross margin rose from 40.0% to 44.0% because revenue grew from $3,000,000 to $3,600,000 while cost of sales increased less quickly, so each same-day procedure retained more after direct costs. The operating margin improved from 14.0% to 16.0%, showing the $480,000 fixed-cost base was absorbed more effectively. Returns on capital climbed from 15.0% to 18.0% even though capital employed rose from $2,800,000 to $3,200,000, meaning the new suite is already adding value. These gains are operational, since operating profit grew despite higher interest payable. The caution is that the 3.4% reprocessing defect rate and 11% absenteeism could push costs up and reverse the trend if the $1,200,000 suite is not managed well.

Conclusion: MHP's financial performance has improved. The gross margin (40.0% to 44.0%), operating margin (14.0% to 16.0%) and returns on capital (15.0% to 18.0%) all rose together on higher revenue and gross profit, not on accounting effects. MHP should protect the gain by cutting reprocessing defects and absence.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three margins/return for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: MHP is considering extending sterile single-use packs across all its day-surgery clinics. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MHP of this decision.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Sterile single-use packs reinforce the infection-control message that 57% of 500 surveyed patients already check, and support the premium wanted by the 68% who would pay $15 more for a same-day slot. That helps protect the $24 contribution per unit on the 60,000 units and strengthens the case for the $1,200,000 suite.

Disadvantage: Single-use packs usually cost more than reusable instruments, which would raise the $18 variable cost per unit unless the $15 premium is accepted on every procedure. The insert gives no figure for the extra pack cost, so the net effect cannot be quantified honestly. Any supply failure would also lift the current 3.4% reprocessing defect rate and lengthen the 6.4-day pre-op wait before the new suite stabilises. Fewer reusable instruments to clean also removes some exposure to the 3.4% reprocessing defect rate at source. Because MHP cannot assume the full $15 premium is won on every procedure, it should pilot the packs on one line and compare defect and complaint figures before a full rollout.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MHP's survey data, costs and quality record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase to $14.60 and the 9.6% rise in sterile-pack input costs will affect MHP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): The increase is 0.75 of a percentage point, so if MHP's $750,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate the extra cost is 0.75% × $750,000 = $5,625 a year (0.0075 × $750,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $480,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it entirely. Higher rates could also make future borrowing for the $1,200,000 suite dearer and slightly dampen the 3.2% growth in demand for same-day slots.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.60 an hour): MHP's workforce of 80 includes hourly-paid clinical support staff, so payroll costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total would be invented and is not given. The defensible test is productivity: 60,000 units ÷ 80 staff = 750 units per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; cutting 11% absenteeism and the 3.4% defect rate and training the 24 untrained staff can help sustain it.

Input cost inflation (9.6%): Sterile packs and disposable kits feed the $18 variable cost on every procedure. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $18 were exposed, 9.6% × $18 = $1.728 per unit, and at 60,000 units that is 60,000 × $1.728 = $103,680 a year. Even a smaller exposed share would erode the $24 contribution on every pack sold.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in sterile-pack input costs will have the greatest impact. It repeats across all 60,000 units and directly attacks the $24 contribution that services the $750,000 loan and funds the $1,200,000 suite, whereas the interest rise costs $5,625 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 750 units per worker. MHP should cut the 3.4% defect rate and seek the $15 same-day premium rather than absorb the full increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to MHP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MHP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
